analysis.one_liner: Ends every federal tax except Social Security payroll taxes after 2000.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 90 cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out all federal taxes — income taxes, corporate taxes, estate taxes, and excise taxes — starting after 2000. The only taxes left standing would be Social Security and railroad retirement payroll taxes. The bill contains no replacement revenue, so it would leave the federal government with no funding for anything except Social Security. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would be the highest earners and corporations, who pay the bulk of federal income taxes. Eliminating the income, estate, and gift taxes would deliver the largest dollar savings to the wealthiest households. Corporations would pay no federal income tax at all.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire Internal Revenue Code except the self-employment, Social Security payroll (FICA), and railroad retirement taxes, ending all income, corporate, estate, gift, and excise taxes after December 31, 2000.
No replacement tax system is provided in the bill, so the changes amount to eliminating nearly all federal revenue rather than swapping one tax for another.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who depends on federal spending would bear the cost: Medicare's non-payroll funding, defense, veterans' benefits, roads, education, law enforcement, and research would lose essentially all their funding overnight. Workers would also keep paying the one tax left — the Social Security payroll tax — while payroll taxes are capped and fall more heavily on middle- and lower-wage earners than income taxes do.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal program beneficiaries and ordinary workers

drawbacks.text: With no replacement revenue, the bill would leave the government unable to fund defense, Medicare beyond payroll contributions, veterans' programs, transportation, education, and law enforcement — either forcing deep cuts or unprecedented borrowing.
The surviving taxes are payroll taxes, which stop applying above a wage cap, so ordinary workers would keep paying taxes while high earners and corporations paid essentially nothing.

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill is a statement rather than a workable plan: it specifies no transition, no substitute funding, and no way to pay for government between its effective date and any future reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the wealthiest households and corporations, the benefits are enormous — the end of nearly all their federal tax liability. For everyone else, the bill offers the same headline of 'no more income tax' while keeping the payroll tax they already pay, and it removes funding for the programs they use. There is no honest way to weigh this as a net gain for working people; the bill reads as a message vote about abolishing the tax code, not a financing plan.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Paxon introduced the bill on September 16, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Ninety members cosponsored the bill — 88 Republicans and 2 Democrats — but the bill received no further committee or floor action.
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in September 1997, and that was the last recorded activity on the bill.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or brought to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, the existing tax system kept funding federal programs as before; no one's taxes changed. Supporters of abolishing the income tax gained a talking point, while anyone relying on federally funded programs was spared the bill's effects.

for.name: Rep. Bill Paxon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 88 of 227 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to terminate all federal taxes except Social Security payroll taxes.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bill Archer, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 88 of the 90 cosponsors — with just 2 Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Repealing the income, estate, and gift taxes would deliver the largest savings to the households that pay the most federal income tax, while payroll taxes — the only ones kept — cap out at high incomes.
The bill ends federal corporate income tax with no replacement, eliminating the tax entirely for companies.
With no income, corporate, or excise tax revenue, funding for defense procurement and other federal contracts would largely disappear, taking jobs with it.
